# Linear hypotheses

One-way analysis of variance, two-way analysis of variance and a polynomial regression are the same normal linear model with different columns in the design matrix. A hypothesis about the coefficients is a set of linear restrictions. The generalised likelihood-ratio test of those restrictions is an $F$ statistic built from the two residual sums of squares.

The simple straight line is [Linear regression](inf-06-regression.qmd). The one-factor split of the total sum of squares is [Analysis of variance](inf-07-anova.qmd). This page is the argument that covers both, and any other linear restriction.

## Matrix form of the normal linear model {#s-matrix-form-of-the-normal-linear-model}

A normal linear model is

$$
Y=X\beta+\varepsilon,
$$

where $Y$ is $n\times 1$, $X$ is a known $n\times p$ matrix of full column rank, $\beta$ is $p\times 1$, and the errors $\varepsilon_i$ are independent $\Normal(0,\sigma^2)$. In one line, $Y\sim\Normal(X\beta,\sigma^2 I)$.

The log-likelihood, up to a constant, is

$$
\ell(\beta,\sigma^2)=-\frac n2\log\sigma^2-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}(Y-X\beta)^\top(Y-X\beta).
$$

For fixed $\sigma^2$ this is maximised by minimising the residual sum of squares. Differentiating with respect to $\beta$ gives the normal equations $X^\top X\beta=X^\top Y$, and

$$
\widehat\beta=(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top Y
$$

when $X$ has full rank. The residual vector is $Y-X\widehat\beta$, and

$$
\mathrm{RSS}=(Y-X\widehat\beta)^\top(Y-X\widehat\beta).
$$

The maximised likelihood at this $\widehat\beta$, with $\sigma^2$ still free, is $(2\pi e\,\mathrm{RSS}/n)^{-n/2}$ up to the usual constant from the normal density. Comparing two nested models therefore reduces to comparing their residual sums of squares. A smaller residual sum of squares is a larger maximised likelihood. Whether the reduction is large enough is the $F$ statistic for a linear hypothesis.

One-way analysis of variance is this model with a column of ones and a column for each group except a reference group, or with any other full-rank coding of the group labels. The coefficient vector holds the reference mean and the group contrasts. The design matrix has $p=J$ columns for $J$ groups, and the residual sum of squares is the within-group sum of squares. The algebra is the same if the groups are written as $\mu+\alpha_j$ with a constraint that makes $X$ full rank. [Two-factor analysis of variance](inf-15-two-factor-anova.qmd) adds columns for the second factor and, when it is present, for the interaction.

## General linear hypothesis {#s-general-linear-hypothesis}

A linear hypothesis restricts $\beta$ by

$$
H_0: R\beta=0
\qquad\text{against}\qquad
H_1: R\beta\ne 0,
$$

where $R$ is a known $r\times p$ matrix of rank $r$. Each row of $R$ is one linear constraint. Testing a single coefficient $\beta_j=0$ uses a row of $R$ that picks out position $j$. Testing that $J$ group means are equal uses $J-1$ contrasts and $r=J-1$.

Let $\mathrm{RSS}_1$ be the residual sum of squares of the unrestricted model, on $\nu_1=n-p$ degrees of freedom. Let $\mathrm{RSS}_0$ be the residual sum of squares of the model refitted under $R\beta=0$, which has $p-r$ free coefficients and $\nu_0=n-(p-r)$ residual degrees of freedom. The difference $\nu_0-\nu_1=r$ is the number of restrictions.

Under the normal model with known $\sigma^2$, the generalised likelihood ratio depends on the data only through $\mathrm{RSS}_0-\mathrm{RSS}_1$. The maximised log-likelihoods differ by

$$
-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}(\mathrm{RSS}_0-\mathrm{RSS}_1),
$$

so $-2\log\Lambda=(\mathrm{RSS}_0-\mathrm{RSS}_1)/\sigma^2$. When $H_0$ is true, $\mathrm{RSS}_1/\sigma^2\sim\chi^2_{n-p}$ and $(\mathrm{RSS}_0-\mathrm{RSS}_1)/\sigma^2\sim\chi^2_r$, and the two pieces are independent. Dividing each chi-squared variable by its degrees of freedom cancels $\sigma^2$:

$$
F=\frac{(\mathrm{RSS}_0-\mathrm{RSS}_1)/r}{\mathrm{RSS}_1/(n-p)}\sim F_{r,\,n-p}.
$$

The level-$\alpha$ test rejects when $F$ exceeds the upper $\alpha$ point of that $F$ law. Large $F$ means the restrictions increased the residual sum of squares by more than sampling variation in $\sigma^2$ can explain.

This is the same $F$ as the analysis-of-variance table. There the unrestricted model gives every group its own mean, $\mathrm{RSS}_1=\mathrm{SS}_{\mathrm{error}}$, and the restricted model forces the means to be equal, $\mathrm{RSS}_0=\mathrm{SS}_{\mathrm{total}}$. The numerator sum of squares is $\mathrm{SS}_{\mathrm{treat}}$. For a straight line, the unrestricted model is $\beta_0+\beta_1 x$ and the restriction $\beta_1=0$ leaves an intercept only. Then $\mathrm{RSS}_0-\mathrm{RSS}_1$ is the regression sum of squares, $r=1$, and $F$ is the square of the slope $t$ statistic.

The table that goes with any such comparison is

| Model | Degrees of freedom | Residual sum of squares | $F$ |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Alternative, $R\beta\ne 0$ | $n-p$ | $\mathrm{RSS}_1$ | |
| Null, $R\beta=0$ | $n-p+r$ | $\mathrm{RSS}_0$ | |
| Difference | $r$ | $\mathrm{RSS}_0-\mathrm{RSS}_1$ | $\dfrac{(\mathrm{RSS}_0-\mathrm{RSS}_1)/r}{\mathrm{RSS}_1/(n-p)}$ |

The null distribution is exact when the errors are independent and normal with common variance, and $X$ is fixed. If the variance is known, $(\mathrm{RSS}_0-\mathrm{RSS}_1)/\sigma^2$ is compared with $\chi^2_r$ directly and the denominator estimate of $\sigma^2$ is unnecessary. In either case the procedure is the [generalised likelihood-ratio test](inf-12-generalised-likelihood-ratio.qmd) for this normal likelihood.

Four points illustrate the arithmetic. Take $x=(1,2,3,4)$ and $y=(2,3,5,6)$. The least-squares line is $\widehat y=0.5+1.4x$. The residual sum of squares is

$$
\mathrm{RSS}_1=(2-1.9)^2+(3-3.3)^2+(5-4.7)^2+(6-6.1)^2=0.20,
$$

on $4-2=2$ degrees of freedom. The intercept-only fit uses $\overline y=4$ and

$$
\mathrm{RSS}_0=(2-4)^2+(3-4)^2+(5-4)^2+(6-4)^2=10.
$$

Then

$$
F=\frac{(10-0.20)/1}{0.20/2}=98
$$

on $(1,2)$ degrees of freedom. The upper $5\%$ point of $F_{1,2}$ is $18.5$, so the test rejects $\beta_1=0$. The slope is not a sampling fluctuation around a flat mean. With $n=4$ the $F$ critical value is large, and a moderate slope would not have cleared it. The formula does not change when $n$ is larger. Only the critical value and the residual degrees of freedom do.

```r
x <- 1:4
y <- c(2, 3, 5, 6)
fit <- lm(y ~ x)
anova(fit)
# Df 1 and 2, Sum of Sq for x equal to 9.8, residuals 0.2, F = 98.
```

## A curve can still be linear in the coefficients {#s-a-curve-can-still-be-linear}

Linearity in the linear model is linearity in $\beta$, not linearity in the covariate. The mean

$$
\E(Y_i)=\beta_0+\beta_1 h_i+\beta_2 h_i^2+\beta_3 h_i^3
$$

is a cubic curve in height $h_i$. It is a linear model because the mean is $x_i^\top\beta$ with the known row $x_i^\top=(1,h_i,h_i^2,h_i^3)$. The design matrix has those four columns. The least-squares estimator and the $F$ test apply without change.

A hypothesis about the shape is a linear hypothesis. No curvature beyond a straight line is $H_0:\beta_2=\beta_3=0$, two restrictions, tested by comparing the cubic model's residual sum of squares with the straight-line model's. No association with height at all is $H_0:\beta_1=\beta_2=\beta_3=0$, three restrictions, tested against an intercept-only fit. A test that the cubic term is unnecessary, leaving the quadratic, is the single restriction $\beta_3=0$.

The same matrix $R$ writes each of these. For dropping the quadratic and cubic terms from a four-parameter fit,

$$
R=\begin{pmatrix} 0&0&1&0\\ 0&0&0&1\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
R\beta=\begin{pmatrix}\beta_2\\ \beta_3\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Nothing in the derivation used the fact that the second and third columns are powers of the first. They could be an indicator for a group, a product of two indicators, or any other numbers fixed before the responses were seen. What they cannot be is a function of $Y$. A column built from the response makes $X$ random in a way the normal equations $X^\top X\beta=X^\top Y$ did not allow, and the $F$ distribution does not apply.

```r
# A cubic in one covariate is lm() with three computed columns.
# The sequential table tests beta3 = 0, then beta2 = beta3 = 0, and so on,
# in the order the columns are added. The extra-sum-of-squares F for a
# chosen restriction is the comparison of the two fitted models, not
# necessarily one line of that sequential table.
h <- c(1.5, 1.6, 1.7, 1.8, 1.9, 2.0)
jump <- c(4.1, 4.4, 4.2, 5.0, 5.6, 5.5)
cubic <- lm(jump ~ h + I(h^2) + I(h^3))
line <- lm(jump ~ h)
anova(line, cubic)   # two restrictions, beta2 = beta3 = 0
```

The numbers in this height example are only large enough to show the syntax. The $F$ statistic `anova` prints is $(\mathrm{RSS}_{\mathrm{line}}-\mathrm{RSS}_{\mathrm{cubic}})/2$ divided by $\mathrm{RSS}_{\mathrm{cubic}}/(6-4)$. With six points and four coefficients the residual degrees of freedom of the cubic are $2$, so the test has very little power. The point of the display is the restriction count, not a conclusion about jumping.

::: {.callout-note}
## Key idea
Write the mean as $X\beta$. A linear hypothesis sets $R\beta=0$. Refit under that restriction, and compare the increase in residual sum of squares with the unrestricted residual mean square. The ratio is $F$ on $(r, n-p)$ degrees of freedom. A polynomial in the covariate is still this model, because the powers sit in columns of $X$ and the unknown quantities remain the coefficients.
:::
